meta.title_plain: How to use AI as a smart helper
meta.teaser: Learn how AI chatbots work and how to make them coach your brain.

page.title: How to use AI as a smart helper: a coach, not a cheat code
page.sub: A skill you can use today
page.bigIdea: AI chatbots like Claude can explain almost anything, any time of day. The trick is using AI to train your brain, not replace it.

cards.title: Know what AI really is
cards.front: A chatbot isn't a brain. So what is it?
cards.back: Chatbots like Claude are large language models. They learned from huge amounts of text. They build answers by predicting the next word, again and again.
cards.tryit: On your phone keyboard, type "The best tennis shot is" and keep tapping the suggested words. That's next-word guessing, mini version.

cards.title: Ask a clear question
cards.front: A vague question gets a vague answer.
cards.back: Say what you want and how. "Explain topspin to a 13-year-old tennis player in 5 sentences" works much better than just "topspin?"
cards.tryit: With Dad, ask an AI the same question two ways: short and detailed. Which answer helps more?

cards.title: Ask it to coach you
cards.front: The best AI tutors don't hand you answers.
cards.back: Sal Khan started by tutoring his cousin online. Later Khan Academy built Khanmigo, an AI tutor that guides you to find answers yourself.
cards.tryit: Pick one maths problem. With Dad, ask an AI: "Give me a hint, not the answer." Then solve it.

cards.title: Check the facts
cards.front: AI can be totally wrong and still sound sure.
cards.back: Sometimes AI makes things up and says them like facts. Experts call this a hallucination. Always check important facts in a second trusted source.
cards.tryit: Ask an AI 3 facts about your favourite tennis player. Check each one on Wikipedia. Were they all right?

cards.title: Keep private stuff private
cards.front: What you type into AI may be saved.
cards.back: Never share your full name, address, school, passwords or friends' photos. Real accounts on most AI tools need an adult, so use them with Dad.
cards.tryit: Write a list of 5 things you would never type into an AI or any app.

words.d: A computer program that does tasks that usually need human skill.
An AI trained on huge amounts of text to write and answer.
The question or instructions you type into an AI tool.
When AI gives false information but sounds sure it's true.
Keeping your personal information safe and to yourself.

quiz.q: How does a chatbot like Claude build its answers?
opts: It looks up one perfect answer in a giant book
It predicts the next word, again and again
A person types every reply really fast
quiz.hint: Think about the phone keyboard test in card 1.
quiz.why: Large language models build answers one word at a time by predicting what comes next.

quiz.q: An AI gives you a fact for a school project. What should you do?
opts: Check it in a second trusted source
Use it straight away, because AI is always right
Ask the AI if it's sure, then use it
quiz.hint: Can AI sound sure even when it's wrong?
quiz.why: AI can hallucinate and still sound confident, so only another trusted source can confirm it.

quiz.q: Which prompt will get you the most useful help?
opts: "Explain how to hit a better backhand slice, in 5 simple steps"
quiz.hint: Which one tells the AI exactly what you want and how?
quiz.why: A clear, detailed prompt tells the AI the topic, the goal and the format you want.

quiz.q: What's the smartest way to use AI for homework?
opts: Ask it to write the whole thing
Ask it for hints and questions while you do the work
Copy its answer and change a few words
quiz.hint: Which choice still makes your own brain do the training?
quiz.why: Handing in work you didn't create can count as cheating, but hints help you really learn.

page.think: Plan your own AI study buddy. What's one thing you want to learn, like a tennis tactic, a maths topic or a Roblox script? Write the exact prompt you'd use so the AI coaches you instead of giving answers.
